title: One life, all humanity
hookLine: whoever saves one life, it is as if he saved all humankind (5:32)

lines: I WILL NOT STRETCH OUT MY HAND.
cards: Two brothers each bring an offering. One is accepted; one is not. The Qur'an doesn't give their names; Muslim tradition calls them Qabil and Habil, the names many people know as Cain and Abel.

The one whose offering was refused says, I will kill you. The other answers with a startling line: even if you stretch out your hand to kill me, I will not stretch out mine to kill you. Then the first brother does it.
Afterward he stands over the body with no idea what to do, until a raven lands and scratches at the ground. That's where today's verse comes from.

teach.b: Surah five, verses twenty-seven to thirty-one, tell the brothers. The raven shows the killer how to hide his brother's body, and he cries out, woe is me, am I not even able to be like this raven?
He's become, the text says, one of the regretful. Then verse thirty-two draws the lesson: for that cause.

In Pickthall's words, whoever kills a human being, except for murder or for spreading corruption in the land, “it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.”
The word for that one life is nafs: a soul, a self, a person.

The Qur'an says this was decreed for the Children of Israel, and the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, teaches something very close: whoever saves one life, scripture counts it as saving a whole world.
A neighbor's sentence, kept in two books. Why one for all? Commentators give a few answers.

Every person comes from the same first parents, so one death breaks the whole family. A person who kills once has shown he'd kill anyone. And the one who saves a life has defended the very idea that life is sacred.
The verse has two halves. People often quote only the first, against killing.
The second is just as large, and it's the one you can do on an ordinary day.

The next verse, thirty-three, deals with armed robbery and war on the community, and commentators read the two together. The heart of thirty-two stays simple: a single person weighs as much as everyone.

how: Muslims often quote 5:32 against murder and terror and in praise of rescuers, doctors and blood donors; scholars teach it together with the story of Adam's two sons in the verses before it and the law in the verse after it.

games.q: your brother tells you he's going to kill you. what does the accepted brother say in the Qur'an?
o: even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won't raise mine.
games.why: he refuses to answer violence with violence, saying he fears Allah, Lord of the worlds (5:28).

practice: Think of a small life near you, easy to overlook: a spider in the corner, a plant that needs water, a friend who went quiet. Pick one, and picture protecting it in one small act: a cup of water, a knock, a text.

wordCard.voice: One life. Nafs: one soul. Surah five, verse thirty-two: to save one life is as if to save all humankind. Today's word.
